concepts.label: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, and its microscopic feature is atrophy of the caudate nucleus with gliosis
concepts.article_title: CAG repeat expansion and caudate atrophy in Huntington disease
concepts.definition: Huntington disease is an autosomal-dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4, producing a mutant huntingtin protein with an abnormally long polyglutamine tract that is toxic to neurons; longer repeat expansions correlate with earlier onset and a phenomenon of anticipation across generations. The disease's characteristic microscopic/macroscopic pathological feature is severe atrophy of the striatum, especially the caudate nucleus (with accompanying gliosis), reflecting selective early neuronal loss there, which underlies the disease's classic triad of chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, with caudate nucleus atrophy as its microscopic feature.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing Huntington disease's caudate/striatal atrophy (from a CAG repeat expansion) with other neurodegenerative diseases' distinct microscopic hallmarks (e.g. substantia nigra Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease) — each neurodegenerative disease has its own genetically and histologically distinct signature.
concepts.original_wording: Source Patho item 1 ("CAG expansion on gene coding for huntegnton protein ----> microscopic feature of disease that cause atrophy of brain (Huntington chorea)"), embedded-answer format, read from CNS Assessment 1.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as CNS Assessment 1's Pathology item 1 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102), p1.

concepts.label: Genioglossus is supplied by contralateral corticobulbar (upper motor neuron) fibres only, unlike most other tongue muscles which receive bilateral supply
concepts.definition: Most muscles supplied by cranial nerve motor nuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar (upper motor neuron) input, so a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion produces little clinical deficit in those muscles. Genioglossus is an important exception: it receives corticobulbar input from the contralateral cerebral hemisphere only. Consequently, a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. a stroke affecting the corticobulbar tract) causes the protruded tongue to deviate toward the side of the lesion (weak genioglossus fails to push the tongue to the opposite, unaffected side) — the basis of the classic "tongue deviates toward the lesion in a UMN lesion, away from the lesion in an LMN (hypoglossal nerve) lesion" clinical rule.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that genioglossus is supplied by contralateral corticobulbar fibres only, unlike most other tongue muscles.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Cranial nerve motor supply
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the tongue-deviation rule for a upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion, where genioglossus's unique contralateral-only supply makes the tongue deviate toward the lesion, with a lower motor neuron (hypoglossal nerve) lesion, where the tongue instead deviates away from the intact side, toward the side of the damaged nerve itself.
concepts.original_wording: Source Anatomy item 6 ("Genoglossus ----> Muscle supplied by contraletral corticobulbar neurons only"), embedded-answer format, read from CNS Assessment 1.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as CNS Assessment 1's Anatomy item 6 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102), p1.

concepts.label: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system
concepts.article_title: Glutamate as the principal CNS excitatory neurotransmitter
concepts.definition: Glutamate is an amino acid that also functions as the principal excitatory neurotransmitter throughout the central nervous system, acting on ionotropic receptors (NMDA, AMPA, kainate) and metabotropic glutamate receptors to mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission at the great majority of excitatory synapses in the brain and spinal cord. This complements GABA, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter, and the balance between glutamatergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition underlies normal CNS signalling; excess glutamatergic activity is also implicated in excitotoxic neuronal injury (for example in ischaemia and some neurodegenerative processes).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing glutamate (the principal excitatory CNS neurotransmitter) with GABA (the principal inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter) — the two are frequently paired in exam questions testing the excitatory/inhibitory neurotransmitter distinction.
concepts.original_wording: Source Biochemistry item 4 ("glutamate ----> principle Excitatory NT ?"), embedded-answer format, read from CNS Assessment 1.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as CNS Assessment 1's Biochemistry item 4 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102), p2.

concepts.label: The substantia gelatinosa (of Rolando) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the spinal cord grey matter
concepts.article_title: The substantia gelatinosa as Rexed lamina II
concepts.definition: Rexed laminae are the ten histologically-defined layers of spinal cord grey matter, numbered I (most dorsal) to X. The substantia gelatinosa (of Rolando), a distinctive band of small, densely packed neurons in the dorsal horn important for modulating incoming pain and temperature signals (the anatomical substrate of the gate control theory), corresponds to Rexed lamina II — immediately deep to the posteromarginal nucleus of lamina I, which relays pain and temperature onward. This lamina II location is present in the dorsal horn at all spinal cord levels, including the cervical segments.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the substantia gelatinosa corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the spinal cord grey matter.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Spinal cord and vertebral levels
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II, pain/temperature modulation) with the posteromarginal nucleus (Rexed lamina I, immediately dorsal to it, chiefly relaying pain and temperature onward) — the two adjacent dorsal horn laminae have related but distinct roles in the pain pathway.
concepts.original_wording: Source Histology item 1 ("SGR in lamina 2 ----> regarding Cervical segment which of the following is true"), embedded-answer format, read from CNS Assessment 1.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as CNS Assessment 1's Histology item 1 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102), p2.

concepts.label: In the Pacinian corpuscle, the sensory nerve fibre runs axially through the centre of the receptor, distinguishing its structure from the Meissner corpuscle
concepts.article_title: The axial nerve fibre of the Pacinian corpuscle
concepts.definition: The Pacinian corpuscle is a large, encapsulated mechanoreceptor with a characteristic "onion-skin" arrangement of concentric lamellae, chiefly responsible for detecting vibration and deep pressure; the Meissner corpuscle is a smaller, more superficial encapsulated receptor for light touch/flutter, with a different internal architecture in which flattened lamellar cells interdigitate around the nerve terminal in a more coiled/branching pattern. A defining structural feature of the Pacinian corpuscle is that its single sensory (afferent) nerve fibre runs axially, straight through the centre of the corpuscle's concentric lamellae, a histological distinction from the Meissner corpuscle's terminal, which does not show this same simple axial course.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the Pacinian corpuscle's sensory nerve fibre runs axially through the centre of the receptor, distinguishing it from the Meissner corpuscle.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the Pacinian corpuscle's structural feature (axial nerve fibre through concentric onion-skin lamellae, detects vibration/deep pressure) with the Meissner corpuscle's distinct structure and function (light touch/flutter, coiled nerve terminal among interdigitating lamellar cells, more superficial location).
concepts.original_wording: Source Histology item 3 ("fibers pass axial in pacinian corpuscle ----> difference between pacinian ane meissener corpuscle"), embedded-answer format, read from CNS Assessment 1.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as CNS Assessment 1's Histology item 3 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102), p2.
